la:num:tres.html:
trēs (also treis and trīs; acc. tres and tris), trĭa, num. adj.
Sanscr. tri-, trajas; Gr. τρεῖς, τρία; Goth. thrija; Germ. drei; Engl. three
.
Three: duas, tris minas auferunt,: tria corpora, Tris species tam dissimiles,: horum trium generum quodvis,: hoc loquor de tribus his generibus,: tribus modis, uno ... altero ... tertio ...,: fundos decem et tres reliquit,.—
To denote a small number: (sermo) tribus verbis,of three words,; so, verbis,. 2, 121; cf. ; : ego tribus primis verbis, quid noster Paetus; at ille, etc.,at the first three words,: haec omnia in tribus verbis,: chartis,: suavia,: cum tribus illa bibit,.

la:verb:tremo.html:
trĕmo, ŭi, 3, v. n. and a.
[cf. Gr. τρέμω, to tremble; ἀτρέμας, quiet].
Neutr., to shake, quake, quiver, tremble, etc. (freq. and class.; cf. trepido): sapiens si algebis, tremes, Novat. ap. (Com.Rel. v. 116 Rib.): pro monstro extemplo'st, quando qui sudat tremit,: viden', ut tremit atque extimuit,: totus Tremo horreoque, Ter Eun. 1, 2, 4: si qui tremerent et exalbescerent objecta terribili re extrinsecus,: timidus ac tremens,: tremo animo,; so, animo,: toto pectore tremens,: corde et genibus tremit, 1, 23, 8.—In a Greek construction: tremis ossa pavore,: ingemit et tremit artus,; cf. .—
Of things: mare caelum terram ruere ac tremere diceres, Afran. ap. Prob. ap. (Com. Rel. v. 9 Rib.): membra miserae tremunt,: genua,: artus, Verg, A. 3, 627: manus,: umeri,: haec trementi questus ore,; so, ore tremente, et saep.: Africa terribili tremit horrida terra tumultu, Enn. ap. Fest p. 153 Müll. (Ann. v. 311 Vahl.): verbere ripae,: aequor,: ilices,: hasta per armos Acta,: vela,: frusta (carnis),i.e. to quiver,: seges altis flava spicis,; .—
Act., to quake or tremble at a thing (mostly poet. and perhaps not ante-Aug.): virgas ac secures dictatoris tremere atque horrere, Liv, 22, 27, 3: Junonem Offensam,: neque iratos Regum apices neque militum arma,: jussa virum nutusque,: te Stygii tremuere lacus,: non praesidum gladios tremunt,: varios casus,: hostem,. — Hence, trĕmendus, a, um, P a. (acc. to II.), that is to be trembled at; hence, fearful, dreadful, frightful, formidable, terrible, tremendous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): manes adiit regemque tremendum,: Chimaera,: vates visu audituque,: oculi,: cuspis,: tumultus,: Alpes,: monita Carmentis,: nefas,: tigris animal velocitatis tremendae,.

la:noun:tremor.html:
trĕmor, ōris, m.
tremo
,
a shaking, quaking, quivering, trembling, tremor.
Lit.
In gen. (class.; cf. trepidatio); terrorem pallor et tremor consequitur,; cf : quo tremore et pallore dixit!: omnia corusca prae tremore fabulor,: gelidusque per ima cucurrit Ossa tremor,: subitus tremor occupat artus,; Ov M. 3, 40: donec manibus tremor incidat unctis,: tota tremor pertemptet equorum Corpora, Verg G 3, 250: errat per artus,. — Plur., .—Personified: Frigus iners illic habitant Pallorque Tremorque,.—
Of inanim. things: dum tremor (ignium) est clarus,. —
In partic., an earthquake: tremor terras graviter pertentat,; ; Claud. ap. .—In plur., ; ; ; ; ; cf. ; .—
Transf., act., like terror, of that which causes trembling, fear, etc., a dread, terror (very rare): (Cacus) silvarum tremor,; cf. : ponti,.

la:adj:trepidus.html:
trĕpĭdus, a, um, adj.
root in Gr. τρέπω, to turn, put to flight; cf. Lat. torqueo (cf. Müll.); prop. scared; hence
,
restless, agitated, anxious, solicitous, disturbed, alarmed, in a state of trepidation, etc. (not. freq. in prose till the Aug. per.; perh. not at all in Cic. and Cæs.): tum trepidae inter se coëunt pennisque coruscant (apes),in a hurry,; so, Dido, Serv.: hic galeam tectis trepidus rapit,; 9, 233: trepidi improviso metu,; cf.: curia maesta ac trepida ancipiti metu,: Romae nocturnus terror ita ex somno trepidam repente civitatem excivit,: trepidi formidine portas Explorant,; . — ( β ) With gen.: illae (apes) intus trepidae rerum per cerea castra Discurrunt,: Messenii trepidi rerum suarum,; so, rerum suarum,: salutis,: admirationis ac metus,: tubarum,. —
Of things: illud (ferrum) in trepidā submersum sibilat unda, (Merkel, tepidā); cf.: et foliis undam trepidi despumat aheni,i. e. bubbling, foaming,: venae,: pes,: ōs,: vultus,: cursus,: terror,: metus,; : tumultus belli,: certamen,: motus,: fletus,: in re trepidā,in a critical situation, perilous juncture,; ; ; cf. in plur.: in trepidis rebus,; ; ; ; ; cf. : incerta et trepida vita,; so, vita,fin.: litterae,i. e. announcing danger, bringing alarming news,; so, nuntius,.—Adv.: trĕpĭdē, hastily, in a state of confusion or alarm, with trepidation: trepide concursans,: classis trepide soluta,; so, relictis castris,: deserta stativa,: trepide anxieque certare,.

la:verb:tremefacio.html:
trĕmĕfăcĭo, fēci, factum, 3, v. a.
tremo-facio
,
to cause to shake, quake, or tremble (poet.): (Juppiter) Annuit, et totum nutu tremefecit Olympum,; : totum caelum supercilio et nutu,: Lernam arcu,: Thulem belli murmure,: se tremefecit tellus, quaked, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 11, 18.—In part. perf.: folia tremefacta Noto,; so, tellus,: pectora,: scuticae habenis,: quies pueri,.

la:verb:trepido.gloss: to hurry with alarm, bustle about anxiously, to be in a state of confusion, agitation, or trepidation
senses: to hurry with alarm, bustle about anxiously, to be in a state of confusion, agitation, or trepidation
la:verb:trepido.html:
trĕpĭdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
[id.], to hurry with alarm, to bustle about anxiously, be in a state of confusion, agitation, or trepidation (class., but not in Cic.): ut ille trepidabat! ut festinabat miser!; so with festinare,; : quid est quod trepidas, Ter Eun. 5, 5, 8: tum demum Titurius trepidare, concursare,: trepidare omnibus locis,: currere per totum pavidi conclave magisque Exanimes trepidare,: dum in sua quisque ministeria discursu trepidat ad prima signa,: trepidante totā civitate ad excipiendum Poenum visendumque,: circa vallum (hostes), Auct. B. Afr. 82, 1: circum artos cavos (mures),: vigiles tumultuari, trepidare, moliri portam,: nobis trepidandum in acie instruendā erat,: dum trepidant alae,: lymphati trepidare coeperunt,: at Romanus homo ... Corde suo trepidat,; : spe trepido,: trepidare laetitiā,, n. 4: voce,: multa manu medicā Phoebique potentibus herbis Nequiquam trepidat,: nam veluti pueri trepidant atque omnia caecis In tenebris metuunt,; ; ; cf.: ancipiti trepidant terrore per urbes,: recenti mens trepidat metu,: metu falso,: formidine belli,: in dubiis periclis,: ridetque (deus), si mortalis ultra Fas trepidat,.—Impers. pass.: trepidari sentio et cursari rursum prorsum,: totis trepidatur castris,: ubi jam trepidatur,: vastis trepidatur in arvis,: si gradibus trepidatur ab imis,.—
Like tremo with acc., to tremble at, be afraid of (poet. and very rare): et motae ad lunam trepidabis harundinis umbram,: occursum amici,: lupos (damae),.—
With inf. (poet.): ne trepidate meas, Teucri, defendere naves,: occurrere morti,.—
With ne: trepidat, ne Suppositus venias et falso nomine poscas,; .—
Of things, : quae (aqua) per pronum trepidat cum murmure rivum,; cf.: obliquo laborat Lympha fugax trepidare rivo,: flammae trepidant,flare, waver, flicker,: trepidantia exta,throbbing, quivering, palpitating,: sic aquilam pennā fugiunt trepidante columbae,: sub dentibus artus,.—
With inf.: octavum trepidavit aetas Claudere lustrum,.—Hence, trĕpĭdanter, adv., trem blingly, timorously, anxiously, with trepidation (rare): trepidanter effatus,.—Comp.: trepidantius timidiusque agere,.

la:verb:tremesco.html:
trĕmesco (trĕmisco), ĕre, v. n. and a.
inch. [tremo], to begin to shake or tremble, to shake, quake, or tremble for fear; to quake or tremble at a thing (poet.): plaustri concussa tremescunt Tecta viam propter,: tonitruque tremescunt Ardua terrarum,: jubeo tremescere montes,: latitans omnemque tremescens Ad strepitum,.—With acc.: sonitumque pedum vocemque tremesco,: Phrygia arma,.—With object-clause: telum instare tremescit,.— With rel.-clause: quercum nutantem nemus et mons ipse tremescit, Quā tellure cadat,.

la:adj:tremulus.html:
trĕmŭlus, a, um, adj.
tremo
.
Lit., shaking, quaking, quivering, trembling, tremulous (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): anus,; cf.: incurvus, tremulus, labiis demissis, gemens,: manus annisque metuque,; so, anni,tempus,: passus (senilis hiemis),: artus,: manus,: guttur, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 8, 14: ut mare fit tremulum, tenui cum stringitur aura,: harundo,: canna,: cupressus,: flamma, Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 43, 110; ; cf.: jubar ignis,: ignes,: lumen,: motus,: horror,: lorum,: colores,: equi,i.e. restless, spirited, (cf. and 250).— Subst.: sacopenium sanat vertigines, tremulos, opisthotonicos, i.e. shaking or trembling in the joints, ; ; .—In neutr., adverb.: (puella) tam tremulum crissat,tremblingly,. —
Transf., act., that causes one to shake or shiver: frigus,.—* Adv.: trĕmŭlē, tremblingly, .

trĕcenti (trĭcenti, ), ae, a (
gen. plur. trecentūm. ; ), num. adj.
tres-centum
, three hundred: nummi Philippii,: Leonidas se in Thermopylis trecentosque eos, quos eduxerat Spartā, opposuit hostibus,: ad trecentos viros trucidavit,: juvenes,: usque ad milia basiem trecenta,

tres-decem
,

senses: the act of trembling or twitching
la:noun:trepidatio.html:
trĕpĭdātĭo, ōnis,
f [trepido], a state of confused hurry or alarm, agitation, confusion, consternation, trepidation (not freq. till the Aug. per.): numquae trepidatio? numqui tumultus? * : quae senatūs trepidatio, quae populi confusio, quis urbis metus,: cujus rei subita trepidatio magnum terrorem attulit nostris, Auct. B. Alex. 75, 2; cf.: nec opinata res plus trepidationis fecit, quod, etc.,: ut jam ex trepidatione concurrentium turba constitit,: pilis inter primam trepidationem abjectis,: trepidationem inicere,: trepidatio fugaque hostium,: vitia non naturae sed trepidationis,: trepidatione mendacium prodere,: ferrum pectori per trepidationem admovens,: vulgi,; in quā trepidatione multae captae naves,: cum magnā trepidatione vigilavit,: nervorum,a trembling,.

la:other:Treveri.html:
Trēvĕri (Trēvĭri), ōrum, m.
A people in Gallia Belgica, between the Moselle and the forest of Ardennes, in and about the mod. Treves, ; ; ; 6, 8 et saep.; ; ; —In sing.: Trēvĭr, one of the Treviri, ; 4, 55; .—In a pun with tresviri, .—
Afterwards, the town of the Treviri, the mod. Treves, ; called, at an earlier date, Augusta Trevirorum,.—
Hence, Trēvĕ-rĭcus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Treveri: ager,; : tumultus,: proelium,: urbs,i. e. Treves,.
